skill.description: Design clear Go structs and interfaces with composition, embedding, type assertions, field tags, dependency injection, and consistent receiver choices.

content.user_title: Design Better Go Structs and Interfaces
content.value_statement: Poor type boundaries make Go code harder to test, extend, and review. This skill applies focused interfaces, useful structs, safe assertions, and clear composition patterns.
actual_capabilities: Recommend small interfaces defined by the consuming package.
Choose between embedding and named fields for composition.
Apply comma-ok assertions and type switches safely.
Select pointer or value receivers with consistent method sets.
Use struct tags, compile-time interface checks, and noCopy guidance.
Prefer concrete constructor returns and generics where types are known.
limitations: It provides design guidance, not a compiler or full static analyzer.
It does not inspect project code unless the surrounding tool grants file access.
It does not choose architecture without the project context and constraints.
It does not replace tests, go vet, race detection, or code review.

use_cases.title: Shape a New Go Package
use_cases.description: Define focused interfaces, concrete constructors, and composable structs for a new package.
use_cases.target_user: Go developers starting a package or service

use_cases.title: Review Existing Type Boundaries
use_cases.description: Find oversized interfaces, premature abstractions, unsafe assertions, and inconsistent receivers.

use_cases.title: Improve Testability Safely
use_cases.description: Introduce consumer-owned interfaces and dependency injection where tests or multiple implementations justify them.

prompt_templates.title: Choose an Interface Boundary
prompt_templates.prompt: I have a Go package with one concrete dependency. Explain whether I need an interface, where it should live, and why.

prompt_templates.title: Review Struct Composition
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this Go struct design and recommend embedding or a named field for each dependency. Explain which methods should be exposed.

prompt_templates.title: Make Assertions Safer
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these Go type assertions and type switches. Replace panic-prone assertions, handle nil values, and preserve optional behavior.

prompt_templates.title: Audit a Type API
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit this Go package for interface size, constructor return types, receiver consistency, struct tags, copy safety, and compile-time interface checks. Give prioritized changes with reasoning.

output_examples.input: A service constructor accepts a storage dependency and currently returns an interface.
output_examples.output: Return the concrete service pointer and accept the consumer-owned storage interface. Callers retain access to the service API while tests can provide a small mock.

output_examples.input: A server embeds a data store but should expose only its HTTP behavior.
output_examples.output: Embed the HTTP handler when its methods should be promoted. Keep the data store as a named field so its internal methods remain private to the server implementation.

output_examples.input: A registry panics when used as its zero value.
output_examples.output: Initialize the internal map lazily in the mutating method. The zero value can then be declared directly and used without a constructor.

best_practices: Define the smallest interface at the point where the behavior is consumed.
Prefer concrete returns, safe comma-ok assertions, and useful zero values.
Run go vet, race tests, and focused round-trip tests after changing type design.
anti_patterns: Do not create interfaces only for hypothetical flexibility.
Do not return interfaces from constructors when callers need the concrete API.
Do not mix receiver styles or use unchecked assertions for recoverable input.

faq.question: Where should a Go interface be defined?
faq.answer: Define it in the consuming package with only the methods that consumer needs.

faq.question: Should constructors return interfaces?
faq.answer: Usually no. Return a concrete type so callers retain its full fields and methods.

faq.question: When should I add an interface?
faq.answer: Add one when a second implementation, consumer, or deliberate test seam requires it.

faq.question: When should I embed a type?
faq.answer: Embed it when the outer type should promote its API. Use a named field for internal use.

faq.question: Why use the comma-ok assertion form?
faq.answer: It turns a type mismatch into a handled branch instead of a runtime panic.

faq.question: Should a Go receiver use a pointer or value?
faq.answer: Use a pointer for mutation, large or lock-bearing structs. Use a value for small immutable values.
